---
title: "research experience"
---

My research journey began during my second summer at Lawrence, when I joined Dr. Brian Piasecki's lab studying cilia function in C. elegans. I quickly moved from supporting a senior student's honors project, characterizing mutant phenotypes using confocal and fluorescence microscopy and dye-filling assays, to working on my own projects. Over two consecutive summers (Ten weeks each) as a Lawrence University Research Fellow, I worked to generate a mapk-15:mCherry recombinant plasmid to co-localize MAPK-15 and CED-1, two proteins implicated in cilia function and neurite pruning. The first summer, using Gibson Assembly, taught me as much through failure: our plasmid construct did not yield the expected product, and I learned the value of systematic troubleshooting and gained a much deeper understanding of the process of genetic cloning. The second summer, with the assistance of Eric Lewellyn, we pivoted to Golden Gate Assembly, which ultimately yielded the recombinant plasmid we had been working toward. Finally seeing those colonies of E. coli grow with my recombinant DNA was frankly euphoric. Now, in my senior capstone project, I am building on this work by developing annexin V staining protocols to validate my own model of the CED-1 and MAPK-15 interaction in neurite pruning. While I won’t have time to validate my model entirely, I hope that other undergraduate students will carry on the project.
